Vernonia amygdalina.name: Bitter Leaf
Vernonia amygdalina.description: A compound and market staple across Nigeria — Ewuro in Yoruba, Onugbu in Igbo, Shiwaka in Hausa. Fresh leaves go into soups, or are squeezed and boiled as a bitter tonic in traditional malaria, digestion, and cleansing practice.

Ocimum gratissimum.name: Scent Leaf
Ocimum gratissimum.description: The fragrant kitchen leaf grown in almost every Nigerian compound. Called Efirin (Yoruba), Nchuanwu (Igbo), and Daidoya (Hausa). Families add it to pepper soup and brew the leaves for cough, fever, and stomach upset.

Moringa oleifera.name: Moringa
Moringa oleifera.description: Drumstick tree leaves sold in markets and grown in yards as Ewe ile (Yoruba) and Zogale (Hausa). A everyday nutrition leaf used as soup green, powder, or tea for strength, immunity, and recovery.

Azadirachta indica.name: Neem
Azadirachta indica.description: Dogoyaro — the neem tree lining streets and compounds across Nigeria. People boil the bitter leaves or bark for fever, malaria, and wash skin complaints. Easy to find; almost every neighbourhood has a tree.

Zingiber officinale.name: Ginger
Zingiber officinale.description: Ata ile — fresh ginger from every Nigerian market and many home gardens. Pounded into tea or pepper soup for colds, nausea, digestion, and body aches.

Hibiscus sabdariffa.name: Zobo
Hibiscus sabdariffa.description: The red calyces behind zobo drink, sold in every market as dry hibiscus. Steeped as a cold or hot drink for refreshment; traditionally used around blood pressure and as a cooling tea.

Allium sativum.name: Garlic
Allium sativum.description: Kitchen garlic (Ayu in Yoruba) found in every stew pot. Crushed raw or boiled in traditional practice for colds, blood pressure, and infections.

Curcuma longa.name: Turmeric
Curcuma longa.description: The yellow kitchen rhizome sold beside ginger in Nigerian markets. Used in food and as a warm tea for inflammation, digestion, and skin.

Psidium guajava.name: Guava Leaf
Psidium guajava.description: Guava trees grow in compounds and along roads. Young leaves are boiled for diarrhoea, stomach upset, and as a mouthwash — a first-aid tree many households already have.

Carica papaya.name: Pawpaw Leaf
Carica papaya.description: Pawpaw grows in almost every Nigerian yard. The unripe fruit and leaves are used in traditional practice for digestion, skin, and recovery drinks.

Garcinia kola.name: Bitter Kola
Garcinia kola.description: Orogbo — chewed at ceremonies and sold on every roadside tray. Traditional use for cough, throat, and as a bitter stimulant; a nut people already keep at home.

Gongronema latifolium.name: Utazi
Gongronema latifolium.description: The bitter soup leaf in Igbo kitchens, sold in every fresh-produce stall. Chewed or added to pepper soup for digestion and blood-sugar traditional use.

Piper guineense.name: Uziza
Piper guineense.description: West African black pepper — uziza leaves and seeds in soups and stews. A market spice used for postpartum recovery, digestion, and colds in traditional kitchens.

Aframomum melegueta.name: Alligator Pepper
Aframomum melegueta.description: Atare — the spice in naming ceremonies and herbal mixtures, sold in every market. Seeds are chewed or boiled for digestion, colds, and as a warming tonic.

Aloe vera.name: Aloe Vera
Aloe vera.description: Potted on balconies and in compounds across Nigeria. The inner gel is used on burns, cuts, and dry skin; a plant many people already grow at the door.

Tamarindus indica.name: Tamarind
Tamarindus indica.description: Tsamiya — the sour fruit pulp sold in northern and southern markets. Used in drinks and porridges, and in traditional practice for fever, digestion, and as a mild laxative.

Vitellaria paradoxa.name: Shea Butter
Vitellaria paradoxa.description: Ori — raw shea from the savanna belt, in every Nigerian soap and skin stall. Rubbed on dry skin, stretch marks, and minor burns.

Adansonia digitata.name: Baobab
Adansonia digitata.description: The baobab of the Sahel and northern Nigeria. Dried leaves (kuka) thicken soup; the sour pulp is a market drink and traditional fever and nutrition food.

Tetrapleura tetraptera.name: Aidan Fruit
Tetrapleura tetraptera.description: The ridged dry fruit in pepper soup and postpartum stews. Sold in spice sections of every southern market; traditionally used after childbirth and for body aches.

Allium cepa.name: Onion
Allium cepa.description: Everyday onion from the kitchen. Warm onion drinks and poultices appear in home care for coughs and colds.

Syzygium aromaticum.name: Clove
Syzygium aromaticum.description: Kanafuru — cloves in every spice box. Chewed or steeped for toothache, cough, and as a warming tea.

Monodora myristica.name: Ehuru
Monodora myristica.description: African nutmeg toasted into soups and pepper soup. A kitchen spice used traditionally for digestion and as a warming postpartum ingredient.

Nauclea latifolia.name: African Peach
Nauclea latifolia.description: Opon / Tafashiya — roots and bark sold in herbal stalls for fever and malaria traditional use. A well-known West African fever tree.

newHerbs.name: Lemon Grass
newHerbs.description: The lemon-scented grass planted along fences and in pots across Nigeria. Families boil a handful as tea for fever, colds, stomach upset, and as a daily evening drink.
newHerbs.preparation: Wash a few fresh stalks, bruise them, and simmer in water 8–10 minutes. Drink as tea, with or without ginger.
warnings: Generally used as food tea; large medicinal doses are not a substitute for malaria treatment.
Stop if you feel dizzy or nauseous.

newHerbs.name: Lime
newHerbs.description: Small green limes from compound trees and every fruit stall. The juice and leaf tea are home care for colds, cough, and as a vitamin-C drink with honey or ginger.
newHerbs.preparation: Squeeze fresh juice into warm water with honey, or boil a few leaves for a short tea.
warnings: Acidic juice can irritate ulcers and tooth enamel.
Avoid undiluted juice on empty stomach if you have gastritis.

newHerbs.name: Cashew Leaf
newHerbs.description: Cashew trees are common in yards and along roads in southern Nigeria. Young leaves and bark are boiled in traditional practice for diarrhoea, toothache, and blood-sugar support.
newHerbs.preparation: Simmer washed young leaves or a small piece of bark 10–15 minutes. Use as a short course tea, not a daily drink.
warnings: Bark teas are astringent — do not use long term.
Nut shell oil is caustic and is not a medicine.

newHerbs.name: Miracle Leaf
newHerbs.description: Abamoda — the fleshy ‘never die’ plant that roots from a fallen leaf on walls, pots, and dumps. A household first-aid leaf for cough, wounds, and ear discomfort in traditional use.
newHerbs.preparation: Warm a washed leaf and apply as a poultice on minor wounds, or squeeze juice for traditional cough use. Do not put leaf juice into the ear if the drum may be damaged.
warnings: Not for pregnancy in medicinal amounts.
Contains cardiac glycosides — do not ingest large quantities.
Seek care for deep wounds or persistent cough.

newHerbs.name: Ringworm Plant
newHerbs.description: Asunwon — the yellow-candle shrub along roads and behind houses. Crushed fresh leaves are a well-known traditional wash for ringworm and other fungal skin spots.
newHerbs.preparation: Crush fresh leaves and rub the juice on the affected skin after washing, once or twice daily. Do not eat the leaves as a laxative without guidance.
warnings: Can irritate broken skin.
Internal use is strongly laxative and unsafe in pregnancy.
See a clinic if the rash spreads or looks infected.

newHerbs.name: Awolowo Leaf
newHerbs.description: The common roadside weed many Nigerians call Awolowo leaf. Fresh crushed leaves are pressed on cuts because they are believed to slow bleeding — a plant you can find on almost any path.
newHerbs.preparation: Wash young leaves, crush, and press on a cleaned minor cut. This is first aid only.
warnings: Use only on minor surface cuts after cleaning.
This plant can cause allergy in some people.
Get medical care for deep wounds, animal bites, or heavy bleeding.

newHerbs.name: Eyin Olobe
newHerbs.description: A small garden and farmland weed used across West Africa as stone breaker. Traditional healers boil the whole plant for kidney discomfort, liver complaints, and fever — easy to pick around homes in the rains.
newHerbs.preparation: Wash a small handful of the fresh plant and simmer 10 minutes. Traditional use is short courses, not endless daily tea.
warnings: Not proven to dissolve kidney stones — seek clinical care for loin pain or blood in urine.
Avoid in pregnancy.
May affect blood sugar.

newHerbs.name: Fluted Pumpkin
newHerbs.description: Ugu — the climbing soup vegetable in eastern and southern kitchens, sold in every fresh market. Leaves are eaten as a blood-building green; traditional use also includes recovery after illness.
newHerbs.preparation: Add washed leaves to soup at the end of cooking, or blend a small handful into a short-boiled drink. Food use is the usual path.
warnings: Seeds must be cooked; raw bitter seeds can be toxic in quantity.
This is food, not a treatment for diagnosed anaemia without medical care.

newHerbs.name: Bitter Melon
newHerbs.description: Ejirin — the bitter climbing gourd on fences and dumps. Leaves and young fruit are used in traditional practice for blood sugar, skin, and malaria support.
newHerbs.preparation: Boil a few washed leaves briefly, or cook the young fruit as a vegetable. Keep portions small — it is very bitter.
warnings: Can lower blood sugar — unsafe with diabetes medicine unless a clinician agrees.
Avoid in pregnancy.
Excess can cause stomach cramps.

newHerbs.name: Bush Mango
newHerbs.description: Ogbono — the soup-thickening kernel in Igbo and southern kitchens, sold in every condiment stall. Food first; traditional talk also covers fullness and body weight.
newHerbs.preparation: Dry-roast and grind the kernels into ogbono soup as usual kitchen practice.
warnings: Food allergen for some people.
Ground seed drinks sold as slimming products are not a medical treatment.

newHerbs.name: African Yellow Wood
newHerbs.description: The bright yellow bark sold in almost every southern herbal market as Awopa. Traditional use is fever, typhoid, and malaria support — a stall herb, not a backyard tree, but easy to find.
newHerbs.preparation: A small sliver of bark is simmered 10–15 minutes. Traditional use is short courses under a practitioner.
warnings: Bitter bark is potent — do not self-dose high amounts.
Not a substitute for laboratory-confirmed typhoid or malaria treatment.
Avoid in pregnancy.

newHerbs.name: Sandpaper Leaf
newHerbs.description: The rough fig leaf used to wash pots and calabashes in many compounds. The same leaf is boiled in traditional practice for ulcers, stomach discomfort, and as a wash.
newHerbs.preparation: Simmer 3–4 washed young leaves 10 minutes. Traditional ulcer teas are short courses.
warnings: Do not scrape skin with the rough leaf as treatment.
Persistent ulcer symptoms need clinical care.

newHerbs.name: Waterleaf
newHerbs.description: Gbure — the succulent vegetable in markets every morning, also growing wild in damp yards. Eaten in soup; traditionally talked about as a cooling, gentle diuretic green.
newHerbs.preparation: Cook as a vegetable in soup or stew. Light cooking keeps it as food rather than a strong medicine.
warnings: High oxalate if eaten raw in large amounts.
This is food, not a treatment for kidney disease.

newHerbs.name: Kola Nut
newHerbs.description: Obi / Oji / Goro — the hospitality nut broken at greetings and sold on every tray. Chewed as a bitter stimulant for alertness; traditional use also for digestion and as a social medicine.
newHerbs.preparation: A small piece is chewed, as in customary hospitality. This is not a children’s snack.
warnings: Contains caffeine-like stimulants — avoid in pregnancy, in children, and with heart rhythm problems.
Can disturb sleep.
Not for people avoiding stimulants.
